It's recommended that you explicitly specify which fields the API should allow in the ordering filter.  You can do this by setting an
`ordering_fields`
attribute on the view, like so:

```
`classUserListView(generics.ListAPIView):queryset=User.objects.all()serializer_class=UserSerializerfilter_backends=[filters.OrderingFilter]ordering_fields=['username','email']`
```

This helps prevent unexpected data leakage, such as allowing users to order against a password hash field or other sensitive data.

If you
don't
specify an
`ordering_fields`
attribute on the view, the filter class will default to allowing the user to filter on any readable fields on the serializer specified by the
`serializer_class`
attribute.

If you are confident that the queryset being used by the view doesn't contain any sensitive data, you can also explicitly specify that a view should allow ordering on
any
model field or queryset aggregate, by using the special value
`'__all__'`
.

```
`classBookingsListView(generics.ListAPIView):queryset=Booking.objects.all()serializer_class=BookingSerializerfilter_backends=[filters.OrderingFilter]ordering_fields='__all__'`
```

If an
`ordering`
attribute is set on the view, this will be used as the default ordering.

Typically you'd instead control this by setting
`order_by`
on the initial queryset, but using the
`ordering`
parameter on the view allows you to specify the ordering in a way that it can then be passed automatically as context to a rendered template.  This makes it possible to automatically render column headers differently if they are being used to order the results.

```
`classUserListView(generics.ListAPIView):queryset=User.objects.all()serializer_class=UserSerializerfilter_backends=[filters.OrderingFilter]ordering_fields=['username','email']ordering=['username']`
```

The
`ordering`
attribute may be either a string or a list/tuple of strings.

A final example of filtering the initial queryset would be to determine the initial queryset based on query parameters in the url.

We can override
`.get_queryset()`
to deal with URLs such as
`http://example.com/api/purchases?username=denvercoder9`
, and filter the queryset only if the
`username`
parameter is included in the URL:

```
`classPurchaseList(generics.ListAPIView):serializer_class=PurchaseSerializerdefget_queryset(self):"""
Optionally restricts the returned purchases to a given user,
by filtering against a `username` query parameter in the URL.
"""queryset=Purchase.objects.all()username=self.request.query_params.get('username')ifusernameisnotNone:queryset=queryset.filter(purchaser__username=username)returnqueryset`
```

For example, you might need to restrict users to only being able to see objects they created.

```
`classIsOwnerFilterBackend(filters.BaseFilterBackend):"""
Filter that only allows users to see their own objects.
"""deffilter_queryset(self,request,queryset,view):returnqueryset.filter(owner=request.user)`
```

We could achieve the same behavior by overriding
`get_queryset()`
on the views, but using a filter backend allows you to more easily add this restriction to multiple views, or to apply it across the entire API.

Note that if a filter backend is configured for a view, then as well as being used to filter list views, it will also be used to filter the querysets used for returning a single object.

For instance, given the previous example, and a product with an id of
`4675`
, the following URL would either return the corresponding object, or return a 404 response, depending on if the filtering conditions were met by the given product instance:

```
`http://example.com/api/products/4675/?category=clothing&max_price=10.00`
```

Typically when using the generic views, you'll override the view, and set several class attributes.

```
`fromdjango.contrib.auth.modelsimportUserfrommyapp.serializersimportUserSerializerfromrest_frameworkimportgenericsfromrest_framework.permissionsimportIsAdminUserclassUserList(generics.ListCreateAPIView):queryset=User.objects.all()serializer_class=UserSerializerpermission_classes=[IsAdminUser]`
```

For more complex cases you might also want to override various methods on the view class.  For example.

```
`classUserList(generics.ListCreateAPIView):queryset=User.objects.all()serializer_class=UserSerializerpermission_classes=[IsAdminUser]deflist(self,request):# Note the use of `get_queryset()` instead of `self.queryset`queryset=self.get_queryset()serializer=UserSerializer(queryset,many=True)returnResponse(serializer.data)`
```

For very simple cases you might want to pass through any class attributes using the
`.as_view()`
method.  For example, your URLconf might include something like the following entry:

```
`path('users/',ListCreateAPIView.as_view(queryset=User.objects.all(),serializer_class=UserSerializer),name='user-list')`
```

When listing objects (e.g. using
`ListAPIView`
or
`ModelViewSet`
), serializers may trigger an N+1 query pattern if related objects are accessed individually for each item.

To prevent this, optimize the queryset in
`get_queryset()`
or by setting the
`queryset`
class attribute using
select_related() (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/models/querysets/#select-related)
and
prefetch_related() (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/models/querysets/#prefetch-related)
, depending on the type of relationship.

For ForeignKey and OneToOneField
:

Use
`select_related()`
to fetch related objects in the same query:

```
`defget_queryset(self):returnOrder.objects.select_related("customer","billing_address")`
```

For reverse and many-to-many relationships
:

Use
`prefetch_related()`
to efficiently load collections of related objects:

```
`defget_queryset(self):returnBook.objects.prefetch_related("categories","reviews__user")`
```

Combining both
:

```
`defget_queryset(self):return(Order.objects.select_related("customer").prefetch_related("items__product"))`
```

These optimizations reduce repeated database access and improve list view performance.

You do not need to write a management command. The functionality you are looking for is already provided by the `drf_create_token` management command.

*   **To generate a token:** Use `./manage.py drf_create_token <username>`. This will return the API token for the user, creating it if it does not exist.
*   **To invalidate/regenerate a token:** If a token has been compromised or leaked, you can regenerate it by passing the `-r` parameter: `./manage.py drf_create_token -r <username>`.

Additionally, you can manage tokens through the Django admin interface. To make this easier with a large user base, you can customize the `TokenAdmin` class in your `admin.py` to use `raw_id_fields`:

```python
from rest_framework.authtoken.admin import TokenAdmin
TokenAdmin.raw_id_fields = ['user']
```

`your_app/admin.py`

llm_response:
This is not a bug. All Django REST Framework (DRF) views are intentionally opted-out of `LoginRequiredMiddleware` because the middleware's behavior of redirecting to a login page is unsuitable for API requests, where a 401 status code is preferred. Additionally, DRF authentication and permission classes may be determined after the middleware has been applied.

To enforce that API requests are logged in, you must configure the following global settings in your `settings.py`:

*   **`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`**: Define the authentication schemes to be used.
*   **`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`**: Set these to require authentication (e.g., `IsAuthenticated`).

By setting these globally, you ensure that API requests are subject to authentication and permission checks, providing the blanket guarantee you require.
llm_references:
If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)
, please note that all views from DRF are opted-out of this middleware.  This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied.  Additionally, when the request is not authenticated, the middleware redirects the user to the login page, which is not suitable for API requests, where it's preferable to return a 401 status code.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings,
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
.  They should be changed accordingly if you need to enforce that API requests are logged in.

The view under test has SessionAuthentication in its authentication_classes. Nothing in my test touches middleware. Why does calling the view directly behave differently under DRF, and what's the right way to write these tests?
reference: In plain Django, CSRF validation runs in middleware, which isn't executed when you test views directly. In DRF it runs inside the view, so the request factory needs view-level CSRF checks disabled — use APIRequestFactory(enforce_csrf_checks=False) (the default) or authenticate with force_authenticate.
reference_contexts: When using REST framework, CSRF validation takes place inside the view, so the request factory needs to disable view-level CSRF checks.
CSRF validation in REST framework works slightly differently from standard Django due to the need to support both session and non-session based authentication to the same views.
llm_response:
Calling the view directly using `APIRequestFactory` behaves differently because it bypasses the middleware stack where authentication and CSRF validation typically occur. When testing views directly, REST framework's `SessionAuthentication` requires the request to be authenticated, and view-level CSRF checks may be triggered.

### Why your tests are failing
1. **Authentication:** `APIRequestFactory` does not automatically handle authentication. Even if `SessionAuthentication` is in your `authentication_classes`, the request object created by the factory lacks the necessary session/user state that the browser provides.
2. **CSRF:** Unlike Django's standard `RequestFactory`, REST framework performs CSRF validation inside the view. By default, `APIRequestFactory` disables this, but if your configuration or view logic expects it, it may cause issues.

### The recommended way to write these tests
The documentation recommends using REST framework's test case classes (such as `APITestCase`), which provide an `APIClient` instance. This client handles the request/response cycle more like a browser, including authentication and middleware, avoiding the need to manually construct requests.

```python
from rest_framework.test import APITestCase
from rest_framework import status

class NoteTests(APITestCase):
    def test_create_note(self):
        # The APIClient handles authentication and middleware automatically
        self.client.login(username='user', password='password')
        response = self.client.post('/notes/', {'title': 'x'}, format='json')
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, status.HTTP_201_CREATED)
```

### If you must use `APIRequestFactory`
If you choose to continue testing views directly, you must manually handle authentication:

1. **Force Authentication:** Use the `force_authenticate()` helper to set the user on the request object.
   ```python
   from rest_framework.test import force_authenticate
   
   factory = APIRequestFactory()
   request = factory.post('/notes/', {'title': 'x'}, format='json')
   force_authenticate(request, user=user)
   response = NoteCreate.as_view()(request)
   ```

2. **CSRF Checks:** If you need to test CSRF validation specifically, you must enable it when instantiating the factory:
   ```python
   factory = APIRequestFactory(enforce_csrf_checks=True)
   ```

`requests`
. This may be useful if:

You are expecting to interface with the API primarily from another Python service,

You want to write tests in such a way that they can also be run against a staging or
